title: How can one rule give {{NAME_5}}'s age from {{NAME_6}}'s age?
description: {{NAME_5}} is three years older than {{NAME_6}}. A letter-number gives one rule for every age, and the rule is used when {{NAME_6}} is twenty three. Keeko doubts that a letter must be one fixed number.
teaching_notes: One idea: a letter-number stands for any age, so one rule covers all ages and is used by replacing the letter with a number. Watch for students who think the letter is one fixed number.

source: {{NAME_5}} is 3 years older than {{NAME_6}}. Use a for {{NAME_6}}'s age and s for {{NAME_5}}'s age
video_script.why: A learner sees that one letter can stand for every age, so a single rule replaces a separate sum for each age.
video_script.substitution: The book's own question about {{NAME_5}} and {{NAME_6}}, with the ages four, ten and twenty three.
video_script.anchor: {{NAME_5}} and {{NAME_6}}, whose ages are always three years apart
video_script.wrong_answer: the letter eigh must be one fixed number
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes the letter eigh as one fixed number, so the rule would fit only one age; the same rule worked for four, ten and twenty three.

final_answer.spoken: the rule is s equals eigh plus three, and {{NAME_5}} is twenty six years old

never_show: the age 26 before the answer beat
maths_rules: When {{NAME_6}} is 4, {{NAME_5}} is 4 + 3. When {{NAME_6}} is 10, {{NAME_5}} is 10 + 3. When {{NAME_6}} is 23, {{NAME_5}} is 23 + 3.
For any age a of {{NAME_6}}, the age of {{NAME_5}} is a + 3, so s = a + 3.
video_script.design: One idea: a letter stands for any age. Assumes adding a number to an age. The stage keeps the two names and the ages four, ten and twenty three; the rule is built on them. Wrong idea: the letter is one fixed number.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; {{NAME_5}} and {{NAME_6}} drawn side by side, with the words three years older between them

marks.p1: the title card From your book arrives
marks.p2: the two children appear with the words three years older
marks.p3: a question mark glows over the age of {{NAME_5}}

narration: <bookmark mark='p1'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='p2'/>{{NAME_5}} is three years older than {{NAME_6}}, and the book wants one rule for the age of {{NAME_5}}.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>The rule should work for every age that {{NAME_6}} may have.
How can we write such a rule?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the age of {{NAME_6}} is shown changing on a small dial while the three years stay fixed; a box marks a letter in place of the changing age

marks.g1: the dial for the age of {{NAME_6}} turns
marks.g2: a box replaces the changing age
marks.g3: the word letter-number is written beside the box

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>{{NAME_6}} may be any age, and the age of {{NAME_5}} changes with it.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>To write one rule for every age, we use a letter in place of the age.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>A letter that stands for a number is called a letter-number.
Its value can change from one case to another.

beats.on_screen: Given: {{NAME_5}} is 3 years older than {{NAME_6}}; a = age of {{NAME_6}}, s = age of {{NAME_5}}

marks.gv1: the first fact is written on the working board
marks.gv2: the letters a and s are written beside the two names

narration: <bookmark mark='gv1'/>Given, {{NAME_5}} is three years older than {{NAME_6}}.
<bookmark mark='gv2'/>Let eigh stand for the age of {{NAME_6}}, and s for the age of {{NAME_5}}.

beats.on_screen: To find: a rule for s using a; the age of {{NAME_5}} when {{NAME_6}} is 23

marks.fd2: the second aim is written under it

narration: <bookmark mark='fd1'/>We find a rule that gives s from eigh.
<bookmark mark='fd2'/>Then we find the age of {{NAME_5}} when {{NAME_6}} is twenty three.
<bookmark mark='s1a'/>When {{NAME_6}} is four, the age of {{NAME_5}} is four plus three.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>When {{NAME_6}} is ten, it is ten plus three.
<bookmark mark='s1c'/>When {{NAME_6}} is twenty three, it is twenty three plus three.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: s = a + 3 ; a + 3 is an algebraic expression

marks.s2a: the three lines of the first step merge into one rule
marks.s2c: the words algebraic expression are written under a + 3

narration: <bookmark mark='s2a'/>In every case, we add three to the age of {{NAME_6}}.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>The age of {{NAME_5}} is eigh plus three, so s equals eigh plus three.
<bookmark mark='s2c'/>An expression such as eigh plus three is called an algebraic expression.

marks.s3a: a is replaced by 23 in the rule

narration: <bookmark mark='s3a'/>To use the rule, replace eigh by twenty three.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>Then s equals twenty three plus three.

beats.on_screen: Answer: s = a + 3, and s = 26 years

marks.ans: 26 years is boxed beside the rule

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>{{NAME_5}} is twenty six years old when {{NAME_6}} is twenty three.
The rule for every age is s equals eigh plus three.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: a must be one fixed number, struck out; the three lines 4 + 3, 10 + 3, 23 + 3 come back beside it

marks.d3: the three lines come back under the rule

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Keeko thinks the letter eigh must be one fixed number, so the rule fits only one age.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>But we used four, ten and twenty three in the very same rule.
<bookmark mark='d3'/>A letter-number can take any value, and each value gives one age of {{NAME_5}}.
